column4: The verse says that one who exchanges faith for disbelief has strayed from the straight way; it makes the section's lost-route image a chosen departure from guidance, not only not knowing a direction.
God brings believers from darkness into light, while false guardians bring others from light back into darkness; this gives the section's light-and-guidance meeting a reversal.
God invites people to the Home of Peace and guides whom He wills to a straight path; this joins the section's shelter, path, and guidance in one statement.
God points out the straight way, while some ways bend; this makes the section's guidance image a distinction between routes, not just a change of light.
God reminds the same addressee that He expanded his breast; this opens another short surah by naming a prior favor before its ease and commands.
God recalls removing the addressee's burden; this adds a past relief to the section's remembered shelter and provision.
The burden had weighed upon his back; this specifies what the relief in 94:2 removed and parallels the section's movement from strain to support.
God says He raised the addressee's mention; this makes the blessing publicly known, beside the section's instruction to tell of a blessing.
The same addressee is promised ease with hardship; this names the relief anticipated by the section's future giving.
The ease-with-hardship assurance is repeated; the repetition makes the promise firm, as the section counts both past provision and what is still to come.
After one task is completed, the addressee is told to strive; this continues the movement from received relief to an action that follows.
The next command is to direct longing to the Lord; it completes 94:7's response to favor with the section's return from reminder to duty.
A person with ample means is to spend accordingly and one with restricted provision according to what God gave; the verse promises ease after hardship, joining giving, need, and delay.
Marriage is encouraged even for the poor, with God's promise to enrich them from His bounty; this directly joins Moses's marriage to the section's passage from need to sufficiency.
The covenant pairs kindness to orphans and needy people with speaking well to others; it brings the section's care of vulnerable people together with its rule for speech.
When relatives, orphans, and needy people attend an inheritance distribution, they are to receive provision and kind words; this joins the section's hand and voice.
Asked what to spend, the answer names parents, relatives, orphans, needy people, and travelers; it gives the asker a concrete answer centered on care.
Asked about orphans, the answer says reforming their affairs is best and that sharing life with them makes them brothers; this gives the section's sheltering image a kinship ethic.
The verse tells guardians who fear injustice toward orphan girls to marry other women; it makes fairness in a household the boundary around the section's orphan-and-marriage images.
Oppressed men, women, and children pray to be brought out of a town and given a protector and helper; this makes shelter a response to domination, as in the section's vulnerable figures.
Satan threatens poverty, while God promises forgiveness and bounty; this counters the fear of need that the section answers with future provision.
After Adam and his wife eat, they become exposed and cover themselves with leaves; this repeats the section's garden fall while making exposure and covering explicit.
Adam and his wife confess that they wronged themselves and ask for forgiveness and mercy; their plea joins being lost to the need for a merciful return.
The couple are sent down to earth, where they will live for a time; this shows the move from the protected garden to a bounded earthly life.
God says people will live on earth, die there, and be brought out from it; the verse joins earthly dwelling, burial, and new creation.
Adam and his wife are sent down and given an earthly dwelling and provision for a time; this is another account of the section's garden-to-need transition.
Adam receives words from his Lord and is forgiven; this supplies a second formulation of loss followed by divine turning.
The descent is followed by a promise that guidance will come and that followers of it need not fear or grieve; this specifies the sheltering effect of guidance.

The tempter promises Adam a tree of lasting life and a kingdom that will not decay; this false promise of permanence sharpens the section's distinction between what is promised and what truly endures.
After eating, Adam and his wife cover themselves with garden leaves; this is the fall's immediate exposure-and-covering scene, before guidance follows in 20:122.
Moses finds two men fighting, one asks his help, and Moses strikes the other; the verse supplies the earlier crisis behind his later description of himself as lost.
Moses asks forgiveness for wronging himself and is forgiven; this makes his later flight and guidance part of a received mercy.
Moses says that because God favored him he will not support wrongdoers; this explicitly turns remembered favor into an ethic, as the section's commands do.
Moses flees the city in fear and asks his Lord to save him from wrongdoing people; this begins the path to Midian as a search for safety.
After Moses says he fled in fear, he says his Lord gave him judgment and made him a messenger; it extends the section's lost-to-guided sequence in Moses's own account.
The youths take shelter in a cave and ask their Lord for mercy and right guidance in their affair; it brings shelter, asking, and direction together.
The youths are told to withdraw to the cave, trusting God to spread mercy and prepare ease; this develops the refuge and guidance petition in 18:10.
God asks who could bring light if night were made perpetual; this states the boundary of the section's movement from covering to visible guidance.
God asks who could bring night if day were made perpetual; the paired reversal completes 28:71's contrast between darkness and light.
By mercy God made night for rest and day for seeking bounty; this joins covering and provision as the section's paired night and daylight do.
Moses strikes a rock and twelve springs flow, with each group knowing its drinking place; this repeats water provision in Moses's story alongside the section's flock at the well.
Each Israelite group receives a known drinking place, shade from clouds, and food; this brings water, shelter, and provision together in Moses's history.
Moses says he leans on his staff and beats down leaves for his sheep; this gives a second concrete pastoral scene beside his encounter with the women's flock.
Abraham asks to see how God gives life to the dead, and is shown birds reassembled and summoned; this makes the section's buried-to-new-creation image visible.
The Hour is certain and God will raise those in the graves; this directly joins the section's buried body to its new creation.
The doubter asks whether God can gather his bones; this names the bodily obstacle raised against the section's promise of renewed creation.
The answer says God can restore even fingertips; this completes 75:3 by specifying the body's reassembly.
The verse points to the earth revived after its death and says the same God will revive the dead; it makes renewal visible in the land.
People ask whether they will be raised after becoming bones and fragments; this names the corpse's apparent finality.
They are told that even if they became stone or iron, God could restore them; this answers 17:49's objection to return.
When they ask who will bring them back, the answer is the One who created them first; this completes the challenge with the first creation as proof.
